juce::CachedValue< Type > Class Template Reference

## Detailed Description

template<typename Type>

class juce::CachedValue< Type >

This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...").

A [CachedValue](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html "This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.") provides an easy way to read and write a [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") property with a chosen type. So for example a CachedValue<int> allows you to read or write the property as an int, and a CachedValue<String> lets you work with it as a [String](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html "The JUCE String class!").

It also allows efficient access to the value, by caching a copy of it in the type that is being used.

You can give the [CachedValue](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html "This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.") an optional [UndoManager](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1UndoManager.html "Manages a list of undo/redo commands.") which it will use when writing to the underlying [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...").

If the property inside the [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...") is missing, the [CachedValue](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html "This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.") will automatically return an optional default value, which can be specified when initialising the [CachedValue](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html "This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.").

To create one, you can either use the constructor to attach the [CachedValue](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html "This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.") to a [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ..."), or can create an uninitialised [CachedValue](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html "This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.") with its default constructor and then attach it later with the [referTo()](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CachedValue.html#a8c492258c48e307ebcbc7f847de57059 "Makes the CachedValue refer to the specified property inside the given ValueTree.") methods.

Common types like [String](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html "The JUCE String class!"), int, double which can be easily converted to a var should work out-of-the-box, but if you want to use more complex custom types, you may need to implement some template specialisations of [VariantConverter](https://docs.juce.com/master/structjuce_1_1VariantConverter.html "This template-overloaded class can be used to convert between var and custom types.") which this class uses to convert between the type and the [ValueTree](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ValueTree.html "A powerful tree structure that can be used to hold free-form data, and which can handle its own undo ...")'s internal var.

juce::CachedValue< Type > Class Template Reference

Detailed Description

template<typename Type>
class juce::CachedValue< Type >

This class acts as a typed wrapper around a property inside a ValueTree.

A CachedValue provides an easy way to read and write a ValueTree property with a chosen type. So for example a CachedValue<int> allows you to read or write the property as an int, and a CachedValue<String> lets you work with it as a String.

It also allows efficient access to the value, by caching a copy of it in the type that is being used.

You can give the CachedValue an optional UndoManager which it will use when writing to the underlying ValueTree.

If the property inside the ValueTree is missing, the CachedValue will automatically return an optional default value, which can be specified when initialising the CachedValue.

To create one, you can either use the constructor to attach the CachedValue to a ValueTree, or can create an uninitialised CachedValue with its default constructor and then attach it later with the referTo() methods.

Common types like String, int, double which can be easily converted to a var should work out-of-the-box, but if you want to use more complex custom types, you may need to implement some template specialisations of VariantConverter which this class uses to convert between the type and the ValueTree's internal var.
